consensus_summary: Pearl chiefly signifies the kingdom of heaven, Christ, salvation, or sacred truth as something of supreme spiritual value; secondary uses include the Church, heavenly glory, and ostentatious wealth.
book_summary: Pearl signifies the full moon: a complete light marking an appointed month and assembly. Revelation’s twelve pearl-gates are correspondingly interpreted as the twelve months, associated with the tribes.
consensus_core_identification: Pearl = supremely precious spiritual reality, principally the kingdom of heaven or salvation.
book_core_identification: Pearl = the full moon and, collectively, a twelve-month calendrical pattern represented by the city’s gates.
boundary_disagreement: The book introduces lunar and calendrical cases absent from every consensus response. It does not merely narrow or broaden the consensus category of supreme spiritual preciousness; it assigns the image to a different referent.
material_contradiction: The book’s reading competes with standard interpretations of the pearl-gates in Revelation 21, reidentifying them as months rather than primarily as signs of heavenly preciousness or glory. Nevertheless, it does not logically disprove the consensus reading of pearls in other contexts such as Matthew 13, so novelty rather than direct contradiction is decisive.
rationale: After reduction, the consensus identifies the pearl with an exceptionally valuable spiritual reality, whereas the book identifies it with the full moon and the annual cycle of twelve months. None of the listed consensus alternatives recognizes this lunar-calendar identification. Shared appeal to Revelation 21:21 does not make the cores equivalent because the proposed referents are materially different.
strongest_objection: The cited texts separately establish that the moon marks appointed seasons and that the New Jerusalem has twelve pearl-gates, but none explicitly equates a pearl with the full moon or the twelve gates with twelve months. Revelation’s immediate twelvefold symbolism is also expressly tribal, making the calendrical correspondence dependent on an unstated inference.
